The industry follows a financial model that is rare -- very @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ costs for labor , materials , inventories , plant and equipment , etc. before -- or concurrently with -- the sale of their products or services . Consequently , their CEOs have a good fix on knowing the cost of their product before they sell it . If the selling price is less than its cost , managers soon learn they have a problem . Hemorrhaging cash is hard to ignore . <p> 8 . When writing P/C insurance , we receive payment upfront and much later learn what our product has cost us -- sometimes a moment of truth that is delayed as much as 30 or more years . ( We are still making substantial payments on asbestos exposures that occurred 50 or more years ago . ) This mode of operations has the desirable effect of giving P/C insurers cash before they incur most expenses but carries with it the risk that the company can be losing money -- sometimes mountains of money -- before the CEO and directors realise what is happening . Certain lines of insurance minimize this mismatch , such as crop insurance or @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and paid . Other lines , however , can lead to executive and shareholder bliss as the company is going broke . Think coverages such as medical malpractice or product liability . In " long-tail " lines , a P/C insurer may report large but fictitious profits to its owners and regulators for many years -- even decades . The accounting can be particularly dangerous if the CEO is an optimist or a crook . These possibilities are not fanciful : History reveals a large number of each species . In recent decades , this " money-up-front , loss-payments-later " model has allowed Berkshire to invest large sums ( " float " ) while generally delivering what we believe to be a small underwriting profit . We make estimates for " surprises " and , so far , these estimates have been sufficient . We are not deterred by the dramatic and growing loss payments sustained by our activities . ( As I write this , think wildfires . ) It 's our job to price to absorb these and unemotionally take our lumps when surprises develop . It 's @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ spurious litigation and outright fraudulent behaviour . Under Ajit , our insurance operation has blossomed from an obscure Omaha-based company into a world leader , renowned for both its taste for risk and its Gibraltar-like financial strength . Moreover , Greg , our directors and I all have a very large investment in Berkshire in relation to any compensation we receive . We do not use options or other one-sided forms of compensation ; if you lose money , so do we . This approach encourages caution but does not ensure foresight . <p> * * * * * * * * * * * * P/C insurance growth is dependent on increased economic risk . No risk -- no need for insurance . Think back only 135 years when the world had no autos , trucks or airplanes . Now there are 300 million vehicles in the U.S. alone , a massive fleet causing huge damage daily . Property damage arising from hurricanes , tornadoes and wildfires is massive , growing and increasingly unpredictable in their patterns and eventual costs . <p> 9 . During my lifetime , auto insurers have generally abandoned one-year policies and switched to the six-month variety . This change reduced float but allowed more intelligent underwriting . <p> * * * * * * * * * * * * <p> No private insurer has the willingness to take on the amount of risk that Berkshire can provide . Amidst the continuing and burgeoning threats of climate change , biodiversity loss , over-exploitation of natural resouces and resultant environmental degradation , an added risk is that of global finance for environmental actions drying up or slowing down . <p> R R RASHMI New Delhi February 22 , 2025 10:16 am <p> Representation image <p> The year 2025 has thrown up new risks for global environmental policies . Amidst the continuing and burgeoning threats of climate change , biodiversity loss , over-exploitation of natural resouces and resultant environmental degradation , an added risk is that of global finance for environmental actions drying up or slowing down . Governments in the developed world are increasingly losing the will and capacity to support the global goals at the cost of the domestic exchequer . <p> They may not have officially downgraded their support for global goals . But their ability and willingness to part with public resources is certainly in question . The announcements made by the new dispensation in Washington DC have rendered @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the world are severely affected by persistent social and military conflicts . In such regions , climate transition pathways are obviously not a priority over the existential questions of survival and reconstruction . The conflicts have lowered the appetite of the developed country governments to deploy resources for the benefit of communities in other regions . A combination of several factors ranging from supply chain disruptions , global energy supply uncertainties , and rising trade protectionism have contributed to the worsening scenario . On the other hand , the demand for more and affordable energy continues to rise in developing countries like India and the need for protection from devastating impacts of environmental degradation is felt more than ever . What then is a possible solution to the pressing question of dwindling global finance for environmental goals . <p> Advertisement <p> Can the markets and other stakeholders fill this gap ? Is it feasible for the governments in the developing world to forge partnerships with private sector entities to secure flow of investments in areas where they need fresh technologies and higher quantum of finance for green transition ? This @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the private sector in environmental actions is usually seen , and rightly so , as an abdication of responsibility of the governments . Also , in most cases this does involve higher costs for the exchequer and the economy . The private sector is not driven by charity in making investments and places priority on covering the financial risks over social benefits . It is in this context that the value of appropriate partnerships between governments and the private sector comes to the fore . @@121559053 <h> Climate Change in Kashmir : A Threat to Biodiversity , Ecosystem Stability , and Measures for Control <p> The effects of climate change are not limited to physical environmental changes ; they extend to species survival Kashmir often referred to as " Paradise on Earth , " is renowned for its rich biodiversity and unique ecological systems . Nestled in the northern part of India , this region has been historically blessed with abundant snowfall , regular rainfall , and a temperate climate that supports a wide range of flora and fauna . However , in recent years , the region has witnessed significant shifts in weather patterns , with reduced snowfall and inconsistent rainfall , which are indicative of the broader impacts of climate change . These changing climatic conditions are having profound implications on the ecosystems of Kashmir , particularly its flora . The regions unique plant species , many of which are endemic or rare , are facing growing threats due to these shifts . Understanding the influence of climate change on this fragile ecological zone is critical , especially for ecologists and botanists who are @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Change on Kashmir 's Ecosystems The effects of climate change in Kashmir are increasingly evident in the following ways : Reduced Snowfall and Altered Rainfall Patterns Traditionally , snowfall in Kashmir would provide a crucial water source , replenishing rivers , lakes , and groundwater . However , this year has seen little to no snowfall , with a reduction in precipitation , which has drastically altered water availability . With less snowmelt to feed the region 's water systems , agriculture , which is heavily reliant on these sources , is facing growing challenges . Additionally , many of Kashmir 's wetlands , which are rich in biodiversity , are at risk due to water scarcity . Rising Temperatures As global temperatures rise , Kashmir is experiencing warmer winters and hotter summers , a trend that disrupts the natural cycles of many species . Plants that rely on cooler temperatures , such as alpine species , are struggling to thrive . The high-altitude ecosystems are particularly vulnerable , as they are sensitive to even slight changes in temperature . These changes alter the blooming patterns , growth rates , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and Reduced River Flow Kashmir 's glaciers , which serve as vital freshwater reservoirs , are retreating at an alarming rate due to rising temperatures . This disruption threatens species that depend on the freshwater ecosystems for survival . Most people living in rural areas , even today , walk around to do their daily business . All the major cities in Europe such as London , Paris , Florence and Geneva began with plans that involved walking to get their work done . Even today , these cities have pedestrian friendly paths , particularly , the cobbled streets in the old town area of these cities . After @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the concept and meaning of distance changed . For more than a hundred years , this has been the template for urban growth . While automobiles began in the US and Europe in the late 19th century , they soon spread to developing countries in the 20th century . With automobiles , road construction also expanded exponentially -- both within the cities and connecting cities . As more and more road length came up , more automobiles were manufactured and owned . Soon , the number of automobiles was far larger than the roads could accommodate , leading to traffic jams in the cities across the world . These were the worst in developing country cities such as Manila , Hanoi , New Delhi , Beijing , Shanghai and Mumbai . This led to a focus on mass transportation such as buses and city metros . With the rise in cars , the emissions of greenhouse gases and the pollution levels in the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ many cities becoming toxic . <p> In the late 20th century and the 21st century , there has been a shift in urban planning to make ' walking to work ' attractive . While open campaigning is not allowed , the process is considered " political " . <p> Voting through a series of secret ballots , each cardinal writes a name of choice on a piece of paper . <p> A two-thirds majority is required to win . <p> Four rounds are held each day until a majority is secured . <p> After each session , the ballot papers are burnt , giving off smoke that can be seen by onlookers . <p> If the smoke is black , the cardinals have failed to reach a decision . White smoke signifies that a new Pope has been picked .

( Image : Pixabay ) <p> Gavin Schmidt , a leading climate modeller and the boss of NASA 's Goddard Institute for Space Science ( GISS ) in New York City , is not noted for his humility . Nevertheless , writing in Nature , a journal , in March 2024 , he confessed to being humbled by his inability , and that of his colleagues , to understand the extraordinary year through which they had just lived -- 2023 had been around 0.2 ? C ( 0.4 ? F ) hotter than had been expected . <p> Not just humbled : worried , too . If climate modellers ' accumulated knowledge and spiffy models could not explain what had just happened , it might mean that climate change had pushed the workings of Earth into @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ operates " . Both the speed of climate change and the workings of the climate might be changing . The future might look even worse than it used to . <p> Nine months later , in Washington DC , Dr Schmidt and his colleagues returned to the subject at a recent meeting of the American Geophysical Union ( AGU ) , the world 's largest annual gathering of Earth scientists . The sessions that took place on the topic felt at times like a murder inquiry , with the evidence for one suspect or another gone through meticulously . The probable verdict is now clearer than it was in March ; some suspects have been ruled out and new clues have emerged which point to some others . The conclusion looks likely to be that the world can expect somewhat higher rates of warming . But the case is still not closed . <p> **45;582;TOOLONG ... It was always going to be hot in 2023 . Climate change forced by greenhouse gases means that all years can now be expected to be warm by past standards ; in 2021 the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ at 0.2 ? C a decade . What is more , the second half of 2023 saw an El Ni ? o get under way . <p> El Ni ? os are the warm phase of a seesaw of winds and ocean currents in the tropical Pacific called ENSO ( El Ni ? o-Southern Oscillation ) . The extra heat that such events can add to the overall warming trend means that El Ni ? o years often set records for global temperatures . Because the El Ni ? o that began in 2023 carried on into the following year , 2024 has therefore ended up being even hotter than the last year ( see chart ) . <h> Whodunnit ? <p> But if not the hottest year on record , 2023 still ranks as the strangest . For one thing , records were tumbling well before the El Ni ? o kicked in in the second half of the year . For another , the scale of the warming compared with the year before was beyond what anyone would normally expect from an El Ni ? o . For @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ basins was very peculiar . <p> At the time , several additional " forcings " were discussed . The underwater eruption of the Hunga Tonga-Hunga Ha'apai volcano in the South Pacific in January 2022 had put a huge amount of water vapour into the normally desiccated stratosphere ; water vapour is a greenhouse gas , and in the stratosphere it sticks around for a long time . The Sun was reaching the peak of its 11-year sun-spot cycle ; during such " solar maxima " , it provides around 0.05% more light than it does on average and its spectrum skews into the ultraviolet . And in 2020 new rules imposed by the International Maritime Organisation ( IMO ) had slashed the amount of sulphur allowed in the fuel of ships on the high seas . <p> Sulphur in ships ' fuel turns into sulphate particles rising from ships ' funnels . Some of those particles end up blowing ashore ; producing fewer of them cleans the landlubbers ' air and saves lives . But the particles also encourage the formation of clouds , brighten clouds already there and reflect @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ any clouds at all : all these effects cool the sea 's surface . <p> As soon as the IMO rules went into effect there were climate scientists keen to see what they did to temperatures . 2023 's spike added to the excitement . At the AGU Andrew Gettelman of the Pacific Northwest National Laboratory in Richland , Washington , presented an overview of studies of the phenomenon . Observations show that the distinctive lines of cloud -- known as " ship tracks " -- that can stretch out behind vessels burning sulphur-rich fuel are indeed much rarer now . Modelling suggests that , overall , this means something like 1.2 more watts per square metre of sunshine are warming the ocean . <p> That is enough to have a significant effect , but not enough to provide all the necessary warming for 2023 . Nor can the concerted action of all the initial suspects suffice . The solar effect is smaller than the fuel effect . The volcano 's effect seems to point the other way . Volcanoes , too , throw sulphur up into the atmosphere . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Corporation , the long-lived sulphate particles created in the stratosphere after the eruption of Hunga Tonga-Hunga Ha'apai more than counterbalanced the warming provided by the water vapour , providing a small net cooling . <p> Evidence against different culprits comes from work published recently in Science . Helge Goessling and his colleagues at the Alfred Wegener Institute in Bremerhaven used satellite data and weather records to show that over the course of this century Earth has gradually been reflecting less sunlight back into space than it used to . 2023 was the dimmest year to date . This was apparently due to paucity of cloud cover , particularly in the northern mid latitudes . <p> Part of this could be down to the new IMO rules , but the dimming is too strong to be explained by that alone . Bjorn Samset of CICERO , a Norwegian climate research institute , points to another possibility : the lack of sulphate emissions is not a result of cleaner ships , but of cleaner Chinese coal-fired power plants . Since 2014 China has been making progress in reducing sulphur emissions by closing @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ flue gases at others . New data leads Dr Samset and colleagues to think the cleanup is having a marked effect across the North Pacific , where cleaner air and fewer clouds will mean more warming . <p> A lung-sparing dearth of sulphates may not be the only thing making Earth less reflective . As the climate warms , its workings change in all manner of ways . One is that the tropics expand , and the tracks of storms in temperate zones narrow . Narrower storm tracks mean less cloud . This sort of shift could be another reason why Earth is growing less reflective , and thus warming more . <p> Both the sulphur stories and the changing cloud patterns suggest that increased warming may be here for some time to come . Models expect warming to speed up as annual emissions get larger , which they continue to do , and as sulphate emissions fall , which they continue to do . Dr Schmidt 's predecessor as the boss of GISS , James Hansen , goes beyond what many of his colleagues are comfortable with when he @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ That said , warming over the decade to 2023 was 0.26 ? C ; not as high as the 0.32 ? C a decade rate that Dr Hansen thinks is the new normal , but well above what it used to be . <p> At the end of the AGU sessions Dr Schmidt felt that there had been real progress on the various possible culprits . In the next few weeks he expects modellers at GISS and elsewhere to start trying to pull them all together into a coherent narrative in new climate-model runs that use the most up-to-date data on both sulphur emissions and the reduction in reflected light . Picking over the results may allow scientists to say with some certainty what actually happened . 
@@121623675 <p> In order to preserve Nagaland 's unique cultural , social and economic characteristics , Article 371A of the Indian constitution grants special provisions to the state . The act states that the central government wo n't interfere in the religious and social practices of the Nagas , their customary laws and procedures , including civil and criminal justice matters , and ownership or transfer of land and resources , unless the state 's legislative assembly passes a resolution to do so . <p> One significant aspect of this provision is the protection of the traditional landholding system of Nagaland . The state follows a communal land ownership system , where land is owned and managed by tribal communities , clans and villages , or even privately held by individuals . However , all types of land are governed by village councils and other traditional institutions . This effectively shields the traditional landholding system from central or state interference . <p> This autonomy in governance also renders local self-governance more powerful in matters of land laws and biodiversity conservation . According to 2021 data , 71% of Nagaland lives in @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ role in planning and managing the economic and social development of the land and the flora and fauna . <h> Land system <p> Neichute Doulo is a social entrepreneur and founder of The Entrepreneurs Associates ( tEA ) , a nonprofit that works on entrepreneurship , including farm-based businesses , in Nagaland . Referring to Nagaland 's unique landholding system , he says : " Many people from outside the state do n't know that we practise village republicanism where villages function independently even today . And that is why you have village councils and its planning arm of village development boards in Nagaland . " <p> For generations now , village councils and village development boards have managed biodiversity conservation , driven by people 's deep connection to the land and nature . Villages in close proximity come together and declare parcels of land as community conserved areas , which they jointly protect from exploitation and degradation . In the past , villages have banned hunting , prohibited the use of explosives and chemicals for fishing , and stopped bushfires and destruction of forests . <p> However , factors @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ have made it more difficult for the councils to effectively continue conservation efforts . These have accelerated the deterioration of the forests and biodiversity , which is hard to navigate for community-level organisations that are limited by budget and resources . <p> Nonprofits that work on environmental conservation in the state point out that community control over land is only the first step in the process . Conservation efforts also require money , and the village councils in the current system are left to find the funds needed for environmental work . Further , it does n't help that these councils have very little support from the state government . <h> Beyond romantic ideals <p> Ruchinilo Kemp , co-founder and chief executive of the Kenono Foundation , a nonprofit that works on biodiversity conservation in Nagaland , believes that we often romanticise community-led initiatives and assume that they will sustain themselves without funding . However , the reality dictates otherwise . While community contributions may suffice for one-time activities , long-term efforts require financial support . <p> He says : " Since the forests are community-owned , the laws dictate @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . In contrast , government-owned forests , wildlife sanctuaries , and national parks receive significant funding for conservation and management . " <p> This means that , currently , community conservation in Nagaland is an additional , unpaid work for people . Ruchinilo shares the example of Sendenyu Community Biodiversity and Wildlife Conservation Board . This village body manages the community conserved area in Tseminyu district 's Sendenyu village and works closely with Kenono . " Our biodiversity guards work for free , but we need to compensate them for their time and effort . They might do it once , but they are juggling this with other commitments such as farming on their land . We must provide honorariums to compensate them for the time spent in conservation efforts . " <p> Notably , conservation is an arduous task for the nonprofits themselves , because institutional funding is hard to come by . Even beyond personnel costs , initiatives such as awareness camps , knowledge sharing and engaging activities require funding and are difficult to pay for . The lack of a unified policy at the state level exacerbates @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ state-level conservation policy in Nagaland , and there 's no centrally allocated budget for the state for maintenance of community land and biodiversity . Many nonprofits in other states apply for grants from the state government under their schemes and policies , but we do n't have that option . " <p> Neichute emphasises that while the state government has allocated funds to address climate change and forest conservation , these funds are currently channelled through existing government departments only . To achieve meaningful impact , he suggests that the government should explore collaborative opportunities with grassroots actors , which could lead to transformative results . <p> Nonprofits such as tEA have tried to draw the attention of the central government and funding agencies to the issues that exist in the state , but the efforts have n't yielded favourable results . <p> In 2008 , tEA started developing a community-led mithun conservation project and took the proposal to government institutions and policymakers in Delhi . Mithun are not only culturally significant to Nagaland , but the animal also plays a critical role in the state 's economy and ecology @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ n't understand the need for such a project in Nagaland . They visited the state but ended up donating boots and jackets to the farmers and made a one-time investment of barbed wire fencing . The problem is that we do n't have enough people from Nagaland in policymaking , and people from outside lack an understanding of our state . " <p> With minimal external support , conservation organisations and nonprofits in Nagaland have been looking for alternatives . They are working on developing innovative solutions such as helping the village communities set up farm-based cooperatives and put aside a portion of the profits for conservation . Some of these efforts have borne fruit . <h> Conservation and entrepreneurship <p> tEA started working on livelihoods and entrepreneurship in 2000 but realised along the way that environmental conservation was a necessity . Neichute says : " The health of our mountain ecosystems is deeply intertwined with the wellbeing of our communities . The condition of our mountain springs , irrigation systems and soil health depend on the state of our forests . As deforestation took its toll , we saw @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ quality . In response , we sought opportunities to integrate livelihood activities with forest conservation , recognising that the two are inextricably linked . " <p> The organisation focuses on mithun rearing in the community land of some villages in Phek district . This is undertaken solely by the members of the community to conserve forest reserves and generate income for the mithun farmers . <p> The nonprofit also runs a plantation programme that aims to plant three billion trees by 2050 . This programme involves closely associating with village councils and elders to identify lands where plantation drives can be carried out . Alongside trees , protection crops such as ginger , turmeric , perilla and job 's tears ( adlay millet ) are distributed to the farmers . Protection crops add to the farmers ' income as they wait for the trees to produce fruits , and act as a cushion in the event of natural calamities impacting the trees . In this manner , the farmers are able to generate an income while rewilding their lands . The organisation also buys back the produce from the farmers @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the Kenono Foundation carries out its conservation work in approximately 80 villages and 20 community forest sites ( each site covers up to three recognised villages ) . <p> Ruchinilo observes that villages like Sendenyu have been proactively conserving biodiversity for 20-25 years , but have received very little assistance from the government or nonprofits . " This means that even if one community conserved area is doing well and another one in a neighbouring village is n't , it affects the environment . <p> 3 . Older cooperatives are difficult to convince : The @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ also working on mindset change . @@121623678 <h> For children : Climate change , global warming and practical solutions that can actually help <h> An excerpt from ' Our Potpourri Planet ' , by Ranjit Lal . Illustrated by Anushua Sinha . <p> While scientists are still trying to wrap their heads around ( and furiously debating ) the question of how exactly life on Earth began , they and we do know about the ingenious plot Mother Nature hatched to ensure that it went on . The first order of the day , was , of course , a reliable , steady source of energy to power up life with . <p> Ah , there was the sun , just 93 million miles away , glowing generously and steadily and providing all the energy ever needed . But this energy , emitted in the form of photons ( light ) , needed to be harnessed . So up she came with the idea of evolving a molecule -- a rather large one -- that could do just that : chlorophyll , which was a soothing green colour ( because it reflected only green light ) and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ pioneering photosynthesisers ) , green algae and green plants . Cyanobacteria , formerly known as blue-green algae , and a minute bacteria , were first off the blocks , photosynthesizing so efficiently that it produced so much oxygen that the era was called the " great oxidation event " . <h> Eventually , oxygen levels stabilised , as much of the cyanobacteria died , but not before multi-cellular life evolved . After this , there was no looking back . It 's thought the first " animals " to emerge were sponges , some 800 million years ago , able to tolerate the now low oxygen levels in the oceans , and then first land plants about 470 million years ago , after which life forms went pretty berserk . <p> To provide sustenance and therefore energy for life , this miracle chlorophyll molecule absorbed carbon dioxide from the atmosphere and sucked up water and water vapour . Using the energy from the photons , chlorophyll split the water into hydrogen and oxygen atoms . It then used the hydrogen in combination with the carbon dioxide to manufacture sugars and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ oxygen it kindly released back into the atmosphere -- this was necessary to burn those sugars and carbs to produce the energy other living creatures need to walk and run and sing and dance , to be alive , to grow and to make more of ourselves ! And brilliantly , every living breathing creature ( and now , alas , too many nonbreathing ones , like cars ! ) emitted the carbon dioxide so vitally needed by plants to live and grow . Which indeed they did , and became the source of our own sustenance , our fuel and food : fruit and vegetables , seeds , tubers and roots . Mammals , reptiles , amphibians , fish , insects -- every living creature dined out on these to fuel their own bodies . Hardcore carnivores simply dined out deliciously on other animals which had become plump and juicy on a plant diet . So , in essence , we are all solar-powered . <p> Alas , we still ca n't manufacture our own food , so are dependent essentially on plants and the animals that eat those @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ imagine the number of Nobel Prizes a scientist would have deserved had they thought of an ideal way for humans to produce their own food ? Okay , so Big Boss Mama Nature got there first , but we can and should use the principle and philosophy behind it -- that what goes around comes around , that nothing goes to waste -- in the way we live today . Because that is the only way that things can work out in the end . <p> We all know that leaves are the storehouses of chlorophyll and leaves grow on trees and bushes , which is why it 's so important to have forests and green areas . In reality , around 50 per cent of the oxygen in the atmosphere is emitted by tiny plankton and other plants floating in the sea . But a good amount of this is used up by marine life and the decomposition that follows when these creatures die . But it 's not all hunky-dory for green plants : their leaves have pores called stomata through which they release oxygen and absorb carbon @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ same pores . In dry places , this can be a problem for the plant , because it needs as much water as it can get . In humid , cool places , you may have noticed beads of moisture beautifully rimming a leaf ( on days when there 's no dew ) in the morning ; this is excess water that the leaf is getting rid of . <h> Ah , I can hear the wheels in your brain whirr and see the gleam in your eye as you prepare to pounce ! If there is more carbon dioxide in the air , wo n't that help plant life -- and therefore us -- to thrive ? The plants will grow bigger and lusher , vegetarians and herbivores will have more to eat and get plumper and juicier , as will carnivores ( and our burgers ) . Best of all , there 'll be more oxygen to go around for everyone ! So , theoretically , would n't cars and other carbon dioxide emitters actually help rather than hinder this process ? <p> Well , for a start @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , reducing their capacity to produce oxygen . Also , we must remember that plants only work the day shift : at night , in the absence of light , they just breathe out carbon dioxide like all the rest of us , which is why we are told not to keep green plants in our bedrooms at night . So , if there 's too much carbon dioxide around , we will all suffocate . The classic candle-in-a-jar experiment will reveal this : the candle needs oxygen to burn and once the oxygen is used up , pfft , the flame goes out ! Yes , that 's not likely to happen to you ( unless you 're locked in a car with the windows rolled up ) because there 's relatively little carbon dioxide in the atmosphere ( compared to other gases ) . But carbon dioxide in collusion with water vapor and other greenhouse gases like ozone and methane acts like a kind of tea cosy over our potpourri planet , trapping and reflecting the heat generated and causing all sorts of problems in those areas of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ they can , such as ice caps and oceans . <p> And with our millions of jets , cars , trains , massive power plants and factories producing everything from silicon chips to bulldozers by the million , all emitting carbon dioxide and other noxious gases in the process , we are physically heating up the planet too : for instance , as much as 60 per cent of the energy produced by an internal combustion engine dissipates as heat , only 30 per cent being used for actual propulsion . Every time anything is burnt it produces carbon dioxide and often other even more dreadful gases like carbon monoxide , nitrous oxides and methane . Most significantly , we get the fuel to burn in our factories and power our luxury cars and aircraft carriers from the fossilised remnants of plants that died millions of years ago , and were buried and compressed under considerable pressure , taking the carbon they contained with them . @@121624482 <p> The IMF working paper Understanding the Macroeconomic Effects of Natural Disasters , authored by Ha Minh Nguyen , Alan Feng , and Mercedes Garcia-Escribano , and published by the International Monetary Fund 's Institute for Capacity Development , explores how natural disasters impact economic growth . With contributions from experts at institutions such as Bank Al-Maghrib and the National Bank of Belgium , the research provides a comprehensive assessment of the macroeconomic consequences of disasters across different income groups and country characteristics . Using data from 1980 to 2019 , the study evaluates how disasters influence output growth and its components , including government expenditure , investment , consumption , imports , and exports . <h> Advanced Economies vs . Developing Nations : A Stark Contrast <p> The study finds that the economic effects of natural disasters vary significantly across income groups . Advanced economies ( AEs ) manage to cushion the blow through a rapid increase in government spending in the same year as a disaster , preventing a significant decline in GDP growth . In contrast , emerging markets and developing economies ( EMDEs ) struggle to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ economic output . Small-island EMDEs , which rely heavily on tourism and exports , are especially vulnerable as infrastructure damages disrupt key industries . <p> On average , GDP growth across all countries declines by 1.3% in the year of a disaster , followed by a partial recovery of 0.8% in the following year . However , this rebound does not fully offset the initial decline , resulting in permanent economic losses . This suggests that while economies may recover in terms of growth rates , they do not regain the full extent of lost economic activity . In non-small-island EMDEs , investment growth is the most negatively affected , while in small-island EMDEs , the biggest impact is on exports , primarily due to infrastructure damage and the decline in tourism . <h> Government Spending : The Key to Economic Stability <p> One of the most striking findings of the study is the critical role of government spending in mitigating the effects of natural disasters . In advanced economies , government expenditure increases by an average of 1.8% in the year of the disaster , helping to stabilize economic @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ private investment and enables faster recovery . <p> In contrast , EMDEs struggle to increase government spending , largely due to limited fiscal space and weaker financial systems . Without a strong fiscal response , these economies experience deeper recessions and slower recoveries . The study also finds that countries with higher pre-disaster fiscal balances ( i.e. , lower debt and stronger government budgets ) are better equipped to handle disasters , as they can deploy emergency funds more effectively . On the other hand , countries with high debt and limited fiscal flexibility face prolonged economic downturns . <h> Why Some Disasters Hurt More Than Others <p> The economic impact of a disaster also depends on its type and severity . The study finds that storms and droughts tend to have faster post-disaster recoveries compared to floods and earthquakes , which cause more prolonged economic damage . The size of physical damage also plays a crucial role -- larger-scale destruction leads to more severe GDP losses . However , the study also finds that larger disasters trigger greater government expenditure responses , particularly in countries that have the fiscal @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ tend to cause more lasting damage due to their heavy reliance on tourism and trade . Many of these economies lack the infrastructure resilience necessary to recover quickly , meaning that even a moderate disaster can lead to years of economic stagnation . Moreover , their geographic isolation and small economic size make it harder for them to attract immediate financial aid and investment for reconstruction . <h> Building Resilience : The Path Forward <p> The study highlights the urgent need for stronger disaster preparedness and financial resilience . Countries with better adaptive capacity -- measured through indices like ND-GAIN -- tend to recover more quickly and suffer less economic damage . However , many EMDEs lack the necessary infrastructure and institutional mechanisms to manage disaster risks effectively . The findings suggest that strengthening fiscal buffers , investing in climate-resilient infrastructure , and improving disaster preparedness can significantly reduce long-term economic costs . <p> For small-island economies and developing countries with limited fiscal space , international financial assistance and risk-sharing mechanisms are crucial . Global initiatives such as climate insurance programs , emergency relief funds , and coordinated disaster response @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . Without adequate intervention , climate-related disasters will continue to widen the economic gap between developed and developing countries , exacerbating global inequalities . <h> A Wake-Up Call for Policymakers <p> The findings of this study serve as a stark reminder of the growing economic risks posed by climate change . While advanced economies have the resources to absorb the impact of natural disasters , poorer nations are left to grapple with persistent economic losses , infrastructure destruction , and slow recoveries . The increasing frequency and severity of natural disasters demand urgent action from policymakers to develop long-term strategies that enhance economic resilience . <p> Global cooperation is essential in addressing the economic consequences of natural disasters . @@121641177 <p> Fashion , a reflection of creativity , identity , and cultural expression , has captivated societies for centuries . From regal silks of ancient dynasties to the iconic trends of the 20th century , clothing has always been a cornerstone of civilisation . However , as consumerism accelerates in the modern era , the fashion industry has undergone a seismic shift . Fast fashion -- a model built on delivering mass-produced clothing at breakneck speed and low cost -- has redefined how clothing is consumed . <p> While fast fashion offers affordability and access to the latest trends , its underbelly reveals a harrowing reality . Behind enticing storefronts and flashy advertisements lies a complex web of exploitation , environmental harm , and waste . The journey of a $10 T-shirt -- from the hands that sewed it to its environmental impact and eventual disposal -- underscores the ethical dilemmas tied to fast fashion 's rise . <p> Labour Exploitation : The Hidden Cost of Affordability <p> Sweatshops and Human Rights Violations <p> Fast fashion 's production largely depends on a workforce in developing nations , where labour rights @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Southeast Asian , house sprawling garment factories employing millions of workers . However , many of these workplaces are fraught with peril . <p> The 2013 Rana Plaza collapse in Bangladesh , a tragedy that killed over 1,100 workers , exposed the industry 's disregard for human lives in its quest for profit . This disaster was not an anomaly but a symptom of a systemic problem where profit margins take precedence over basic human rights . <p> Women : The Backbone of the Garment Workforce <p> Women make up nearly 80 per cent of the global garment workforce , a statistic that highlights their pivotal role in the fast fashion supply chain . Yet , their invaluable contributions are overshadowed by systemic injustices . These women often find themselves in low-wage positions with little to no opportunities for career advancement . In many factories across developing countries , they earn wages far below what is needed to support their families , let alone break the cycle of poverty . <p> Workplace harassment is another grim reality . Reports of verbal abuse , sexual harassment , and physical intimidation are @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ or losing their jobs . Many female garment workers also face ' double burdens ' -- long hours in factories followed by household responsibilities , leaving them with little time for rest or personal growth . <p> Despite these challenges , women continue to work in this sector because it provides a semblance of financial independence , even if limited . Organisations advocating for fair wages and safe working environments are slowly making progress , but the journey towards equity remains arduous . <p> Cycles of Poverty and Debt Bondage <p> For many garment workers , especially in rural or marginalised communities , factory jobs are not merely a source of income but a form of survival . However , recruitment practices in some countries bind workers into exploitative arrangements . Agencies charge exorbitant fees to secure jobs , leaving workers indebted before they even begin earning . <p> Once employed , workers are often coerced into excessive overtime to repay these debts , effectively trapping them in modern-day slavery . In extreme cases , they may be unable to leave their jobs without risking financial ruin or retaliation from @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of labour laws , allowing exploitation to persist unchecked . <p> Lack of Visibility for Consumers <p> The fast fashion industry 's success depends heavily on its ability to mask these grim realities from consumers . Glossy advertisements and trendy storefronts distract shoppers from the human cost behind their purchases . The garments women and children labour over often travel thousands of miles before reaching shelves , disconnecting buyers from the exploitation embedded in each stitch . <p> Awareness campaigns , ethical brands , and advocacy groups are working to bridge this gap . By shedding light on the struggles faced by women in the garment industry , they empower consumers to demand better practices and support initiatives that protect vulnerable workers . <p> A Call for Change <p> Addressing these issues requires a multi-pronged approach : stricter enforcement of labour laws , increased transparency in supply chains , and empowering women through education and fair wages . With global awareness and consumer demand for ethically produced clothing on the rise , the industry has the opportunity to transform . Women deserve dignity , security , and equity in the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ essential . <p> Environmental Damage : The Price Paid by Our Planet <p> Pollution and Resource Depletion <p> The environmental footprint of fast fashion is enormous . The production of textiles accounts for about 20 per cent of global wastewater and 10 per cent of global carbon emissions , making it one of the most polluting industries . Polyester , the most widely used fabric in fast fashion , is derived from fossil fuels and contributes to microplastic pollution in oceans . <p> Meanwhile , cotton farming consumes staggering amounts of water . It takes 2,700 litres of water to produce a single cotton shirt -- enough for one person to drink for 2.5 years . The heavy use of pesticides in cotton cultivation further depletes soil health and endangers ecosystems . <p> Carbon Emissions and Climate Change <p> The High Carbon Cost of Fast Fashion <p> Fast fashion 's environmental impact is staggering , with carbon emissions being one of its most critical concerns . Every stage of a garment 's lifecycle contributes significantly to climate change , from raw material extraction to final disposal . The energy-intensive processes @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , are major culprits . Polyester , derived from petroleum , dominates the market due to its low cost and durability , but its production emits nearly three times more carbon dioxide than natural fibres like cotton . <p> Additionally , the industry 's reliance on fossil fuels for machinery , dyeing processes , and electricity further amplifies its carbon footprint . Post-production , the global transportation of garments -- from factories in Asia to retailers in Europe , the Americas , and beyond -- relies on carbon-heavy modes such as shipping and air freight . Frequent restocking to meet ever-changing trends exacerbates this issue , making fashion one of the most polluting industries globally . <p> Estimates suggest that the fashion industry is responsible for 10 per cent of annual global carbon emissions , more than aviation and maritime shipping combined . If no significant interventions are made , emissions could rise by 50 per cent by 2030 , pushing the planet closer to the brink of environmental collapse . <p> Water Use and Methane Emissions in Disposal <p> Adding to the carbon problem is the improper disposal of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ longevity , degrade poorly in landfills , releasing methane -- a greenhouse gas 25 times more potent than carbon dioxide -- as they break down over centuries . The rise of microplastics from synthetic fibres washed into water systems during laundering also worsens ecological harm , infiltrating food chains and marine ecosystems . <p> Landfills Overflowing with Waste <p> The Disposable Fashion Phenomenon <p> Fast fashion 's emphasis on affordability and fleeting trends has cultivated a throwaway culture . Clothing is now considered disposable ; garments are purchased inexpensively , worn a handful of times , and discarded once they fall out of style or deteriorate in quality . On average , a single person discards 37 kilograms of textiles annually , resulting in approximately 92 million tons of textile waste globally each year . <p> A significant portion of this waste ends up in landfills , where it occupies valuable space and contributes to severe environmental pollution . Natural fibres such as cotton or wool may decompose eventually , but the process is often hindered by synthetic dyes and chemical finishes , which release harmful substances into the soil @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ nylon , commonly used in fast fashion , can take hundreds of years to degrade . <p> Incineration : An Unseen Polluter <p> When not sent to landfills , textile waste is often incinerated . While burning garments may reduce physical waste volume , it comes with its own environmental hazards . The process emits toxic fumes , including carbon dioxide , nitrogen oxides , and sulphur dioxides , worsening air quality and contributing to acid rain . The incineration of chemically treated textiles can also release carcinogens , posing health risks to nearby communities . <p> Exporting Waste to Developing Nations <p> In a troubling twist , a large portion of discarded garments from developed countries is shipped to developing nations under the guise of ' charitable donations ' . These shipments often consist of low-quality , unsellable clothing , burdening recipient countries with managing foreign waste . In some areas , the influx of secondhand clothing disrupts local economies , undermining indigenous textile industries . <p> Reframing Consumer Behaviour to Combat Waste <p> Tackling fast fashion 's waste problem begins with consumer behaviour . Shoppers must be encouraged @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , and embrace sustainable practices like repairing , repurposing , or donating garments . Brands , too , have a critical role to play by embracing circular economy principles -- designing products for longevity and recyclability while minimising waste during production . <p> In addition , the industry is beginning to see innovative solutions , such as clothing made from biodegradable or recycled materials , but these efforts must scale significantly to counterbalance the current crisis . Global regulations and consumer advocacy are needed to ensure fast fashion moves toward sustainability , reducing its toll on landfills and the planet . <p> Consumer Behaviour and Fast Fashion Hauls <p> The Role of Social Media in Promoting Overconsumption <p> The advent of social media has redefined shopping culture , particularly with the rise of " fast fashion hauls " . Platforms like Instagram , TikTok , and YouTube teem with influencers showcasing their latest purchases -- dozens of outfits often bought in a single shopping spree . These videos , designed to entertain and inspire , glamorise excessive consumption and reinforce the idea that clothing is disposable . <p> Young audiences @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ often drawn into a cycle of purchasing clothes not out of necessity but for the fleeting satisfaction of owning something ' new ' . This trend is fuelled by fast fashion brands offering dirt-cheap prices and constant discounts , making it easier for consumers to buy in bulk . The psychological effect is significant -- many individuals develop a ' buy now , discard later ' mindset , contributing to wastefulness . <p> Furthermore , the algorithm-driven nature of social media amplifies this culture . Users are shown targeted advertisements and similar haul content , perpetuating the cycle of consumption . The societal pressure to keep up with influencers and peers compounds the problem , leading to wardrobes filled with items often worn once or twice before being discarded . <p> The Environmental Impact of Haul Culture <p> This consumption pattern is not just financially unsustainable for individuals but also devastating for the planet . The increased demand for trendy , low-cost clothing fuels overproduction , leading to excessive use of natural resources like water and energy . Overproduction also results in unsold inventory , much of which ends up @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . <p> Additionally , the rapid turnover of trends driven by haul culture means that garments are rarely designed for durability . Poor-quality materials and cheap production methods ensure that clothing deteriorates quickly , further emphasising their disposability . <p> The Global Secondhand Clothing Crisis <p> A False Solution to Fast Fashion Waste <p> In wealthier nations , donating unwanted clothing to thrift stores or charities often creates a sense of doing good . However , the reality is far more complex . The sheer volume of discarded garments exceeds local demand , leaving charities overwhelmed . Much of this excess is exported to developing countries under the guise of secondhand donations . <p> Countries in Africa , Southeast Asia , and South America have become dumping grounds for fast fashion waste . While some clothing is reused , much of it is unsellable due to poor quality or unsuitable styles . This results in piles of textile waste clogging local landfills , waterways , and streets . <p> Economic and Cultural Implications <p> The influx of cheap , secondhand clothing disrupts local textile industries , as imported garments are @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ not compete with . This undermines traditional craftsmanship and the livelihoods of local workers , leading to economic dependency on foreign imports . <p> Culturally , the dominance of Western secondhand clothing often overshadows indigenous styles , eroding cultural identities . In some regions , this has sparked debates about whether accepting secondhand imports is a sustainable practice or a form of environmental colonialism . <p> Efforts to Manage the Crisis <p> Some countries , such as Rwanda and Kenya , have implemented policies to restrict or ban secondhand clothing imports , aiming to revive local industries and reduce environmental burdens . However , these measures are often met with resistance from exporting nations that view secondhand trade as a way to manage their textile waste . <p> On a positive note , initiatives focusing on upcycling and repurposing secondhand garments are gaining traction . These efforts not only reduce waste but also provide creative opportunities for local artisans to turn discarded clothing into valuable products . <p> A Shift in Mindset Is Necessary <p> Both haul culture and the secondhand clothing crisis underscore the urgent need for systemic change @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and towards valuing garments for their quality , craftsmanship , and longevity . Governments , brands , and individuals -- all have roles to play in addressing the environmental and social harm perpetuated by these practices . The fashion industry must embrace circular economy models and prioritise sustainability , while consumers must learn to make mindful choices that reflect an awareness of the broader implications of their shopping habits . <p> Cultural Implications : Exploitation and Appropriation <p> The Exploitation of Indigenous Creativity <p> Fast fashion often capitalises on cultural motifs , patterns , and traditions without understanding their origins or meanings . This practice , known as cultural appropriation , is widespread in the industry . Brands borrow designs from indigenous cultures such as African mud cloth , Indian block printing , Mexican Otomi embroidery , and Peruvian textile traditions , mass-producing them without acknowledgment or fair compensation to the original communities . <p> For example , African mud cloth , a centuries-old textile made from fermented mud dyes in Mali , carries deep symbolic meanings within its patterns , often used to tell stories or denote social status @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , with artisans using hand-carved wooden blocks to create intricate patterns that have been perfected over generations . Fast fashion frequently replicates these designs , stripping them of their cultural significance and reducing them to fleeting trends . <p> This exploitation goes beyond mere design replication ; it commodifies sacred and symbolic elements , transforming them into profit-generating items while erasing their historical and spiritual significance . For indigenous communities , these patterns and motifs are more than aesthetics -- they embody stories , identities , and rituals . The lack of acknowledgment in fast fashion perpetuates a narrative where cultural heritage is consumed without respect for its roots . <p> Impacts on the Communities of Origin <p> The mass-market reproduction of these designs undermines the authenticity of artisanal crafts . When brands sell cheap knockoffs of these textiles , the artisans who created the original designs lose their economic foothold . This not only deprives them of income but also discredits their craftsmanship , making it harder for them to sustain their practices in a market flooded with imitations . <p> Loss of Artisanal Traditions <p> The Displacement of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the heart of many cultures , preserving not only creativity but also community identity and history . For instance , handwoven fabrics are often replaced by machine-made replicas that can be churned out at a fraction of the cost . <p> As demand for fast fashion grows , fewer artisans can compete in a market dominated by low-priced goods . Young generations , observing the diminishing economic viability of these crafts , are less likely to continue their family traditions , leading to a gradual erosion of centuries-old skills . Organisations and ethical brands are working to ensure that artisans receive fair pay and recognition for their work . Governments in some regions are also stepping in to provide funding and support for traditional craftspeople , recognising their importance as cultural ambassadors . <p> By investing in and purchasing directly from artisans , consumers can play a vital role in sustaining these crafts . It is crucial for the fashion industry to move towards collaboration rather than exploitation , integrating artisanal traditions respectfully into modern design without compromising their authenticity . This shift can help ensure @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . <p> The circular economy emphasises reusing , repairing , and recycling clothing to extend its lifecycle . Brands like Patagonia and Eileen Fisher have pioneered initiatives to refurbish used garments , reducing the demand for new production . <p> The Role of Consumers <p> Mindful Shopping <p> Consumers have the power to drive change . By choosing quality over quantity , supporting ethical brands , and resisting the urge for impulse purchases , they can reduce the demand for fast fashion . <h> Conclusion <p> Fashion is more than what people wear -- it reflects their values and choices . While fast fashion offers the thrill of affordability and trendiness , it comes at a profound ethical cost . Behind every bargain lies a story of exploited workers , a damaged planet , and a culture of waste . However , hope is not lost . By supporting sustainable practices , advocating for fair trade , and rethinking consumption habits , society can collectively pave the way for an ethical fashion industry . @@121641179 <p> Tetra Pak announced their offering of packaging material with certified recycled polymers , becoming the first company in the food and beverage packaging industry in India to do so . Its carton packages integrating recycled polymers are certified by ISCC PLUS ( International Sustainability &amp; Carbon Certification ) , a globally applicable sustainability certification system . The packaging material integrates 5% certified recycled polymers , as mandated by the Ministry of Environment , Forests &amp; Climate Change , under the Plastic Waste Management ( Amendment ) Rules 2022 . This mandate comes into effect on April 1 , 2025 . <p> This milestone marks a significant step in the company 's commitment to circularity , focusing on reducing dependence on fossil-based resources and maximising material reuse . In addition , it remains dedicated to responsibly sourcing raw materials , designing packages for enhanced recycling and reduced litter , and building strong partnerships to develop effective collection and recycling infrastructure worldwide . <p> Cassio Sim ? es , managing director , Tetra Pak South Asia , said , " We are proud to be the first carton packaging producer to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . We applaud the commitment of the Ministry of Environment Forests &amp; Climate to promoting circularity , and for making India one of the first countries in the world to introduce this regulation as early as 2025 . This is an opportunity for all of us in the food &amp; beverage industry to collaborate closely , and transition to more circular solutions . " <p> The ISCC PLUS ( International Sustainability &amp; Carbon Certification ) certified recycled polymers are sourced and allocated to the solutions according to the ISCC mass balance attribution method . Using chemical recycling technology , the plastics are made of a mix of recycled and non-recycled materials , with the corresponding mass of recycled materials tracked throughout the supply chain . These chemically recycled plastics comply with the same global food contact regulations as virgin polymers . From a quality perspective , chemically recycled plastics are equivalent to fossil-based plastics . <p> Using recycled material can contribute to increased @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ content mandates across the world , including India , offer a regulatory push to ensure producers buy recycled materials ; this increases demand and thereby encourages expanded offer . @@121666831 <p> The South Sudan Natural Resources Review , published by the World Bank Group , provides an in-depth analysis of the country 's vast natural resources , highlighting both their immense potential and the risks posed by weak governance , climate change , and economic instability . South Sudan is home to some of the world 's richest renewable natural resources . Its fisheries , forests , and wildlife support millions of people , yet they remain underutilized and poorly managed . The country 's White Nile floodplain and Sudd wetland sustain one of the most productive freshwater fisheries globally . The oil sector , which currently dominates the economy , has caused pollution and deforestation , with mining expansion potentially worsening these issues . Weak governance and widespread corruption continue to impede sustainable resource management . Without institutional reforms and stricter regulations , the benefits of South Sudan 's natural wealth may remain out of reach for its citizens . Investing in cold storage , improving transport infrastructure , and regulating exports could significantly boost revenue and job creation in the fisheries sector . @@121667859 <p> The Thames , the iconic English river that flows through London , will witness a potential increase in algal blooms in the coming years courtesy climate change , a new study has warned . <p> This will happen even though the river 's water has seen a dramatic reduction in phosphorus loads in the last 40 years , as per the analysis . Controlling phosphorus from sewage discharges and agricultural runoff is a key strategy to reduce algal blooms in rivers and lakes , because the algae require phosphorus to grow . <p> " Despite huge successes in reducing phosphorus loads in the River Thames , phosphorus concentrations remain above levels that would limit algal growth and rising water temperatures are now increasing the potential for algal blooms in the river . Our results suggest that water quality management is now ' treading water ' in a warming climate , " Jarvie said . <p> She added that her research documented 150 years of remarkable changes in river water quality . This was of particular importance and timeliness given the challenges the world now faced in managing water quality in a warming climate , and contemporary water quality concerns in Britain and around the world , she observed .

The Indian Legacy of Pluralism and Coexistence <p> India 's history is a rich tapestry woven with threads of diverse cultures , religions , and philosophies , each contributing to the vibrant mosaic of its civilization . This legacy of pluralism and coexistence is deeply rooted in the ancient Indian ideal @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of nation , creed , and caste dissolve , and humanity is united in a shared bond of kinship . This principle , which transcends geographical , cultural , and religious boundaries , reflects the inclusive ethos of Indian civilization . It is a call to recognize the inherent unity of all humanity , despite apparent differences . The Vedas , Upanishads , and other sacred texts of India have long emphasized this unity amidst diversity . For instance , the Rig Veda proclaims : " Let us have concord with our own people , and concord with people who are strangers to us ... May we unite in our minds , unite in our purposes , and not fight against the divine spirit within us " ( Atharva Veda 7.52.1-2 ) . This verse encapsulates the spirit of harmony and mutual respect that has been a hallmark of Indian thought for millennia . <p> The Indian tradition of pluralism is not merely a philosophical ideal but a lived reality . Throughout its history , India has been a sanctuary for various religious and cultural traditions , from Hinduism , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , and Zoroastrianism . The ancient edicts of Emperor Ashoka , who ruled in the 3rd century BCE , exemplify this commitment to coexistence . Ashoka , after embracing Buddhism , promoted principles of non-violence ( ahimsa ) , compassion , and respect for all religious traditions . His rock edicts declare : " All religions should reside everywhere , for all of them desire self-control and purity of heart " ( Rock Edict XII ) . This message of tolerance and mutual respect remains a cornerstone of India 's cultural heritage . <p> The Upanishads , which form the philosophical foundation of Hinduism , further reinforce the idea of unity in diversity . The famous dictum Tat Tvam Asi ( Thou art That ) from the Chandogya Upanishad ( 6.8.7 ) teaches that the essence of the individual self ( atman ) is identical to the universal reality ( Brahman ) . This profound insight underscores the interconnectedness of all beings and serves as a spiritual basis for pluralism . Similarly , the Bhagavad Gita , a text revered by millions , emphasizes the importance of seeing the divine @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ all beings , and all beings in the Self , sees truly " ( 6.29 ) . This vision of universal oneness encourages individuals to transcend narrow identities and embrace a broader sense of kinship with all life . <p> In modern times , figures like Swami Vivekananda have championed India 's legacy of pluralism and coexistence on the global stage . In his famous 1893 speech at the Parliament of the World 's Religions in Chicago , Vivekananda declared : " I am proud to belong to a religion which has taught the world both tolerance and universal acceptance . We believe not only in universal toleration but we accept all religions as true . " This statement , rooted in the teachings of the Vedanta philosophy , reflects the essence of India 's spiritual heritage . Vivekananda 's message was not merely about tolerance but about celebrating the diversity of religious paths as different expressions of the same ultimate truth . His words continue to inspire millions , reminding the world of the importance of dialogue , understanding , and mutual respect . <p> The Indian tradition of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and architecture , which often blend elements from different cultures and religions . For example , the Sufi tradition in India , with its emphasis on love and devotion , has deeply influenced Indian music , poetry , and spirituality . The poetry of Kabir , a 15th-century mystic , exemplifies this syncretic spirit . Kabir , who drew from both Hindu and Islamic traditions , wrote : " The river is one , though the banks are different . " His verses celebrate the unity of all spiritual paths and critique the divisions created by dogma and ritual . Similarly , the architectural marvels of India , such as the Taj Mahal and the Golden Temple , stand as symbols of the country 's ability to harmonize diverse cultural influences into a cohesive whole . <p> India 's legacy of pluralism and coexistence is not without challenges . The country has faced periods of conflict and division , often fuelled by political , social , or economic factors . The Indian Constitution , adopted in 1950 , enshrines the principles of secularism , equality , and fraternity , reflecting @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the freedom of religion , affirming that " all persons are equally entitled to freedom of conscience and the right freely to profess , practice , and propagate religion . " This constitutional framework provides a strong foundation for building a peaceful and inclusive society . <p> The Indian tradition of pluralism also offers valuable lessons for the global community . In a world grappling with polarization and conflict , the concept of a global family and shared nest offers a compelling reminder of our collective humanity . The wisdom of the Vedas , Upanishads , and other sacred texts , complemented by the inspiring examples of visionaries like Ashoka ( BCE 304-232 ) , Kabir ( 1398-1518 ) , and Vivekananda ( 1863-1902 ) , highlights that diversity can be a powerful catalyst for growth , strength , and enrichment , rather than division . By embracing pluralism and coexistence , societies can cultivate deeper understanding , cooperation , and peace , ultimately fostering a more harmonious world . <p> India 's journey toward pluralism and coexistence is ongoing , requiring constant effort and vigilance . It calls for @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ as well as a willingness to confront and address the forces of division and hatred . The words of Mahatma Gandhi ( 1869-1948 ) , one of India 's greatest champions of pluralism , remain relevant : " I do not want my house to be walled in on all sides and my windows to be stuffed . I want the cultures of all lands to be blown about my house as freely as possible . " ( Young India , June 1 , 1921 ) This vision of openness and inclusivity is at the heart of India 's legacy and serves as a guiding light for the future . <p> The Indian legacy of pluralism and coexistence is a testament to the enduring power of unity in diversity . Rooted in ancient scriptures and exemplified by historical figures and modern leaders , this legacy provides a strong foundation for building a peaceful and harmonious society . It challenges individuals and communities to look beyond differences and recognize the common humanity that binds us all . Challenges to Peace in Contemporary India <p> India , with its rich spiritual heritage and legacy of pluralism , has long been a beacon of coexistence and harmony . However , the nation faces significant challenges to peace in the contemporary era , which threaten to undermine its social fabric and collective well-being . These challenges are multifaceted , rooted in political , social , economic , and environmental issues , and they demand urgent attention and thoughtful solutions . <p> One of the most pressing challenges is the rise of identity-based politics , which often exploits divisions along the lines of caste , religion , and ethnicity . While India 's diversity has historically been a source of strength , it has also been manipulated for political @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Politicians and groups sometimes use divisive rhetoric to mobilize support , creating an " us versus them " mentality that deepens societal fractures . This politicization of identity not only erodes trust between communities but also distracts from pressing issues such as development , education , and healthcare . The consequences of such divisive politics are evident in incidents of communal violence , which leave lasting scars on the nation 's social fabric . Addressing this challenge requires a renewed commitment to the principles of unity and inclusivity that have long been central to India 's ethos . <p> Another significant challenge is the proliferation of misinformation and hate speech , particularly on social media platforms . While the internet has democratized access to information and enabled free expression , it has also become a breeding ground for falsehoods and inflammatory content . Misinformation spreads rapidly , often fuelling fear , suspicion , and hostility between communities . Hate speech , whether directed at religious , caste , or ethnic groups , exacerbates existing tensions and can incite violence . The anonymity and reach of social media make it difficult @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ these platforms often prioritize sensational content , further amplifying divisive narratives . Combating this issue requires a multi-pronged approach , including stricter regulation of online content , public awareness campaigns to promote media literacy , and efforts to foster a culture of responsible communication . <p> Economic inequality is another major obstacle to peace in contemporary India . Despite significant economic growth in recent decades , the benefits of development have not been evenly distributed . A large portion of the population continues to live in poverty , lacking access to basic necessities such as clean water , healthcare , and education . This disparity exacerbates social tensions , as marginalized groups feel excluded from the opportunities and resources available to others . Economic inequality often intersects with other forms of discrimination , such as caste and gender , creating a cycle of disadvantage and resentment . Addressing this challenge requires inclusive policies that prioritize the needs of the most vulnerable , as well as efforts to create equitable opportunities for all . <p> Environmental degradation is another critical challenge that threatens peace and stability in India . The country @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , air pollution , deforestation , and soil degradation . These issues not only harm the environment but also have severe social and economic consequences . For instance , water scarcity can lead to conflicts between communities , while air pollution contributes to health problems and reduces quality of life . Climate change exacerbates these challenges , increasing the frequency and intensity of natural disasters such as floods and droughts . The impact of environmental degradation is particularly severe for marginalized communities , who often depend on natural resources for their livelihoods . Addressing this issue requires sustainable development practices , stronger environmental regulations , and greater public awareness of the importance of conservation . Initiatives such as the Swachh Bharat Abhiyan ( Clean India Mission ) and the National Solar Mission are positive steps , but a more comprehensive and coordinated approach is needed to tackle the scale of the problem . <p> These challenges highlight the need for a renewed commitment to the ethical and spiritual values that have historically sustained Indian society . The principles of ' the world is one family ' , ahimsa ( non-violence @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ religions ) offer a roadmap for navigating these complex issues . These values emphasize the importance of unity , compassion , and respect for all life , providing a moral framework for addressing the root causes of conflict and division . <p> Education also plays a crucial role in fostering peace and social cohesion . By promoting critical thinking , empathy , and a sense of shared responsibility , education can help counter the forces of division and hatred . Schools and universities should incorporate lessons on India 's pluralistic heritage , as well as the importance of tolerance and mutual respect . Civil society organizations , religious leaders , and community groups also have a vital role to play in promoting dialogue and understanding between different groups . <p> Ultimately , building a peaceful and inclusive India requires collective effort and a shared vision for the future . It calls for political leaders to prioritize the common good over narrow interests , for citizens to reject divisive narratives and embrace their shared humanity , and for policymakers to address the structural inequalities that fuel social tensions . The challenges @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ provide a strong foundation for overcoming them . <p> In conclusion , while contemporary India faces significant challenges to peace , these challenges also present an opportunity for renewal and transformation . By drawing on the ethical and spiritual values that have sustained Indian society for centuries , and by addressing the root causes of conflict and division , India can continue to be a model of pluralism and coexistence for the world . The path to peace is not easy , but it is one that India must tread with determination and hope , guided by the timeless principles of unity , compassion , and justice . <p> 4 . The founding leaders included former President Josip Broz Tito , former Prime Minister of India Jawaharlal Nehru , former Egyptian President Gamal Abdel Nasser , former Ghanaian President Kwame Nkrumah and Indonesia 's former President Sukarno . @@121709059 <h> India must strengthen its statistics for a new era of data-driven governance <p> Amitabh Kant , Ranveer Nagaich 4 min read26 Feb 2025 , 02:00 PM IST <p> India 's economic success in the coming decades will depend on how well we collect , interpret and use data to drive progress . ( istockphoto ) <h> Summary <p> The country 's economic future depends on harnessing the power of data . Strengthening the National Sample Survey ( NSS ) can enable us to achieve this vision . Here 's what needs to be done . <p> This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you . Subscribe to enjoy similar stories . <p> Reliable statistical insights were virtually non-existent when India was still establishing itself as a newly independent nation . The setting up of the National Sample Survey ( NSS ) in 1950 marked a defining moment in India 's post-independence economic planning . Spearheaded by Professor P.C. Mahalanobis , the NSS was designed to bridge critical data gaps in key economic and social indicators . Since its inception , the NSS has been the backbone of evidence-based @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ C.R. Rao , Debabrata Lahiri and V.M. Dandekar , the NSS evolved into a world-class statistical system . In 1951 , its scope was expanded to urban India . In 1955 , NSS crop cutting experiments ( CCE ) became the gold standard in estimating agricultural yields . <p> Data collection was institutionalized by the formation of the National Sample Survey Organisation ( NSSO ) in 1970 . Since the 1980s , the NSS has widened its ambit to include health , education and informal-economy studies . <p> Aligning with global statistical standards , the independence , transparency and accessibility of NSS data has aided governments , researchers , private enterprises and civil society alike .
